section.title: The dashboard: speedometer and odometer
section.p: Look at two instruments on a car dashboard.
The odometer records distance. It tells how many miles the car has accumulated.
The speedometer records speed. It tells how fast the odometer reading is changing.
For the moment, imagine that the car moves only forward along a straight road. Then speed and velocity agree. Later, when the car can reverse direction, we will need signed velocity.

figure.caption: The odometer records accumulated distance. The speedometer records how fast that distance is changing.

The notation d(t) means: the distance depends on the time. When the input is a time t, the output is a distance d(t). We will soon give this kind of rule a name: a function. For now, the notation lets us keep track of the trip.

subsection.title: Distance as accumulated motion
subsection.p: Suppose the odometer reads 18{,}246.3 miles at 9{:}00 and 18{,}346.3 miles at 11{:}00. During those two hours, the car has accumulated
miles.

The odometer does not say how the car traveled those 100 miles. The driver might have gone steadily. Or slowly at first and quickly later. The odometer remembers the total effect, not the moment-by-moment history.
If we reset the trip odometer at the start, then d(0)=0. After 2 hours in this example,
The distance function d(t) is a memory of the trip.

statement.p: Two trips can produce the same odometer change even if one is steady and the other is stop-and-go. In your own words, what information does a distance function d(t) remember, and what information does it throw away?

hint.p: Think of d(t) as a running total. A total can be the same even when the path that produced it was not.

subsection.title: Velocity as changing distance
subsection.p: Velocity measures how fast distance changes.
If the car travels 100 miles in 2 hours, then its average velocity over that time is
Using d(t), this is

This number is an average over an interval. It does not say that the car was moving at exactly 50 miles per hour at every instant. It only says that the total change, spread evenly over two hours, would be 50 miles per hour.
A speedometer asks a sharper question:
subsection.md: \text{How fast is the distance changing right now?}
subsection.p: That word “right now” is where calculus enters.

exercise.title: What does an average velocity hide?

statement.p: If a car travels 100 miles in 2 hours, the average velocity is 50 miles per hour. In your own words, why is that number not yet a speedometer reading, and what extra question does the word right now add?

hint.p: An average spreads a total change over a whole interval. A speedometer asks about one instant inside that interval.

exercise.title: What do the units already tell you to do?

statement.p: Distance is measured in miles and velocity in miles per hour. In your own words, why do those units force velocity to be a ratio of a change in distance to a change in time, and why does multiplying velocity by time return a distance?

hint.p: Treat units as instructions: division by hours makes a rate; multiplication by hours undoes that division.

exercise.title: How can a whole distance record produce a velocity at one instant?

statement.p: Starting from a known function d(t), we look at fractions such as \frac{d(2.001)-d(2)}{2.001-2}. In your own words, what are those fractions measuring, and why should shorter and shorter time intervals be better clues to the velocity at t=2?

hint.p: Each fraction is still an average, just over a smaller window. Ask what that window is trying to collapse onto.

exercise.title: How can a velocity record rebuild distance?

statement.p: If velocity is not constant, we break a trip into pieces and add products of the form velocity times time. In your own words, why does each such product give a piece of distance, and why does adding the pieces reconstruct the odometer change?

hint.p: On a short piece where velocity hardly changes, the constant-velocity rule is a good local story. Accumulation is the act of adding those local stories.

subsection.title: The two questions together
subsection.p: The two questions are opposite in spirit.
means: measure the instantaneous rate of change.
means: accumulate many small changes.
The first process will be called differentiation. The second will be called integration. The deepest early theorem in calculus will say that these two processes undo each other.

exercise.title: Why are the two dashboard questions inverses?

statement.p: One question goes from distance to velocity; the other goes from velocity to distance. In your own words, why should these two processes undo each other, and what would go wrong in the story if they did not?

hint.p: If you accumulate a rate of change, you should recover the original change. If you measure how fast an accumulated quantity is changing, you should recover the original rate.

subsection.p: For now, we test the story in the simplest case: constant velocity.
